title: Review: Nucleic acids; Origins of cells; Cell structure

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Genetic code
items.clue: The rules by which a base sequence is translated into an amino acid sequence.

items.label: Fluorescent stains
items.clue: Dyes that absorb light of one wavelength and emit light of a longer wavelength.

items.label: Resolution
items.clue: The smallest distance between two points at which they can still be seen as separate.

items.label: Phosphate group
items.clue: The acidic, negatively charged component of a nucleotide, bonded to the pentose sugar.

questions.stem: Part of one strand of a DNA molecule has the base sequence ATGGCA. What is the base sequence of the complementary strand at the same position?

options.text: ATGGCA
TACCGT
UACCGU
GCAATG

questions.explanation: Each base on one strand is paired with its complement on the other: A with T, T with A, G with C and C with G. So ATGGCA is paired with TACCGT.

questions.stem: Which row correctly gives differences between DNA and RNA?

options.text: DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, thymine.
DNA: two strands, ribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, ribose and uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: two strands, ribose, uracil.

questions.explanation: DNA is double-stranded, contains the pentose deoxyribose and has thymine; RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and has uracil in place of thymine.

questions.stem: How does complementary base pairing allow the genetic information in a DNA molecule to be replicated?

options.text: Each separated strand is a template on which free nucleotides pair by hydrogen bonding, so both new molecules keep the original sequence.
Each separated strand acts as a template on which free nucleotides pair by covalent bonding, so both new molecules carry the original sequence.
Each strand is copied directly, base for base, so the new strand is identical to the strand it was built against, preserving the sequence.
Only one strand acts as a template, because the other strand has the same base sequence and would give exactly the same product if it were copied too.

questions.stem: How many different base sequences are possible for a single DNA strand that is 10 nucleotides long?

options.text: 4 × 10, which is exactly 40
10⁴, which is exactly 10 000
4¹⁰, which is about 1 000 000
2¹⁰, which is exactly 1024

questions.explanation: Each of the 10 positions can be any of four bases, independently of the others, so the number of possible sequences is 4 × 4 × … (10 times) = 4¹⁰ = 1 048 576.

questions.stem: With the ×40 objective lens in place, 40 divisions of an eyepiece graticule line up exactly with 100 µm on a stage micrometer. Using the same objective, a cell spans 44 graticule divisions. What is the actual length of the cell in millimetres?

options.text: 1.1 mm

questions.stem: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across. They cannot be seen with a light microscope but are clearly visible in electron micrographs. What is the reason?

options.text: The electron microscope magnifies many more times, so much smaller objects become visible.
Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so the resolution is much higher.
Heavy-metal stains used for electron microscopy make small structures much sharper.
Electron microscopes use fluorescent stains that make ribosomes glow in the dark.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the structure of a DNA molecule?

options.text: Two antiparallel strands linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, A with T and G with C.
Two strands with identical base sequences linked by hydrogen bonds between matching bases.
Two antiparallel strands linked by covalent bonds between complementary base pairs, A–T and G–C.
Two parallel strands linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, A with T and G with C.

questions.stem: A student sketches the ring structures of ribose and deoxyribose. Which difference should the sketch show?

options.text: One carbon of the deoxyribose ring has an extra –OH that ribose lacks.
The deoxyribose ring has six carbon atoms where the ribose ring has five.
The rings are identical, and the sugars differ only in which base is attached.
One carbon of the deoxyribose ring carries –H where ribose carries –OH.

questions.explanation: Deoxyribose is ribose with one hydroxyl group replaced by hydrogen, so it has one fewer oxygen atom. The sketch shows –H at that carbon in deoxyribose and –OH in ribose.

questions.stem: The template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGGA at one position. What base sequence will the mRNA transcribed from it have at that position?

options.text: UACGGA
AUGCCU
ATGCCT
CGUAAG

questions.explanation: RNA nucleotides are added by complementary base pairing with the template: A pairs with U, T with A, C with G and G with C. So TACGGA gives AUGCCU.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the capacity of DNA for storing information is described as limitless?

options.text: Capacity is not limitless: with only four bases, DNA can store far less than a code with more symbols could.
Each position can be one of only two base pairs, but the molecule is long enough to make up for the small alphabet.
A DNA molecule can be of any length and have any base sequence, so the number of possible sequences has no upper bound.
Each nucleotide added creates four more possible sequences, so a long molecule stores a great deal.

questions.stem: A student focuses a stained temporary mount at low power, then rotates the high-power objective lens into place. The image is now slightly blurred. What should the student do?

options.text: Turn only the fine adjustment until the image is sharp.
Turn the coarse adjustment, since it changes the focus most quickly.
Add more stain to the mount so the structures show up clearly.
Switch to an even higher-power objective lens to enlarge the details.

questions.explanation: At high power the objective is close to the slide and the depth of focus is very small, so the fine adjustment is the only focusing control used; it moves the lens by tiny amounts to sharpen the image without risk to the slide or lens.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of cryogenic electron microscopy over conventional electron microscopy?

options.text: Rapid freezing keeps unfixed, unstained molecules near their natural state, so structures are resolved in near-atomic detail.
Heavy-metal stains bind more firmly at very low temperature, so the contrast between structures in the specimen is much greater.
Freezing makes the cell brittle, so it can be fractured to reveal the interior of its membranes in section.
The very low temperature prevents the electron beam from killing the cells, so living cells can be observed in action.

questions.stem: A variety of carbon compounds is thought to have formed spontaneously on pre-biotic Earth. Why do the same processes not produce these compounds naturally on Earth today?

options.text: Carbon compounds can only be produced by the metabolism of living cells.
The atmosphere now contains free oxygen, which oxidizes such compounds as they form.
Oxygen was present then as now, so something else must have stopped the processes.
The same reactions occur today, but living organisms consume the products first.

questions.stem: Which of these is the smallest unit that can sustain itself as living, given only nutrients and a source of energy?

options.text: A whole multicellular animal
A virus inside a host cell
A mitochondrion in a cell
A free-living bacterium

questions.explanation: A bacterial cell carries out metabolism, growth, response, homeostasis and reproduction using its own enzymes, genetic material and membranes. The cell is the smallest unit of self-sustaining life.

questions.stem: In ribosomes, the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids is catalysed by ribosomal RNA. Why is this significant for hypotheses about the origin of cells?

options.text: It shows that RNA is more stable than DNA, which is why it survived from the earliest cells.
It shows that rRNA must be a protein, since only proteins can act as catalysts.
It shows that DNA came first, because the rRNA is transcribed from genes in DNA.
It shows that RNA can catalyse reactions, as presumed for the earliest cells.

questions.stem: Which evidence supports the existence of a last universal common ancestor (LUCA)?

options.text: The same genetic code and some shared genes are found in all organisms.
All organisms carry identical DNA sequences in each of their genes.
Fossils of LUCA itself have been identified in the oldest rocks on Earth.
DNA extracted from the oldest known fossils matches the genomes of modern organisms.

questions.explanation: The IB guide names the universal genetic code and shared genes across all organisms as the evidence for LUCA. Both are features that are best explained by inheritance from a single common ancestor.

questions.stem: Stromatolites and microfossils in rocks from Western Australia are among the oldest evidence of cells. Which approach is used to estimate their age?

options.text: Carbon-14 dating of the carbon left in the fossilized cells themselves
Sequencing the DNA preserved in the fossils and applying a molecular clock
Identifying the fossils as LUCA and reading its age from the family tree
Radiometric dating of the rock using isotopes with very long half-lives

questions.explanation: The rock containing the fossils is dated from the decay of long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, giving an age of about 3.5 billion years and so a minimum age for life on Earth.

questions.stem: Which pair of findings provides evidence that LUCA evolved in the vicinity of hydrothermal vents?

options.text: Photosynthetic microfossils in rocks formed in shallow sunlit water, and light-harvesting genes shared by all organisms
Microfossils in ancient seafloor vent precipitates, and conserved genes across all life that fit vent conditions
DNA sequenced from vent microfossils, and its close match to the genomes of bacteria living at vents today
A fossil of LUCA itself recovered from a vent chimney, together with the age of the surrounding rock
